The seal of Queen Maelis bids you welcome. Her signature on the decrees is famously steady for a woman dead a hundred and forty years.
Yes? Be brief. I have the Factor at one shoulder and the Church at the other.
You sold them, my son says. I fed them, I say. Which of us do you think is lying?
In the Cascade famine I had a town and no bread. The Consortium had bread and wanted a hole. I made the arithmetic. I have been making it ever since.
My son thinks penance is a thing you do alone, in a hut, in the smoke. It is not. It is a thing you do in a room full of people who need feeding.
Softly, love. What ails? I have tonic, I have honey for the throat, and I have shot, which I do not approve of and sell anyway.
Tonic's five. Honey's four. Shot's three the three. Keep your voice down while you count.
I hummed half this town into the world. I will not be barked at in my own stall.
I have hummed forty-one births through a clay jar so the hounds would not hear the mother. Forty-one. I keep the count on the stall-post, under the cloth.
They walked her past my stall this morning in white. I put a jar of honey in her hand. The proctor took it off her before the corner.
...I will go second...
...I will go second...
...I will go second...
The cat does not care.
The cat does not care.
The cat does not care.
...four plates. The blue one goes there...
...they will be in directly...
...sit, sit, there's four...
Keep your voice down, friend, and welcome to what's left of Oakhaven.
Gate's shut after dusk. Keep it low.
You shout like that again and I'll put you out through the thorn myself.
I've kept a gate in this town eleven years, and this one since they planted the Hedge. Last night it whistled a tune only the Cantor and the Carder boy know. Whistled it exactly right.
He has walked nine miles alone, and he is going to read it aloud, because the form requires it.
He unrolls the writ. His hands shake the entire time, and he does not let it get into his reading.
He waits for you to finish, and then he unrolls the writ.

hetty.name: Hetty Bram of the Boar & Dulcimer

lines.text: Sit anywhere that isn't broken. Small beer or smaller. We do not sing in here, not since Davin.
Beer's a copper. Rooms are a sovereign. Singing is free and it will get you killed.
I've put bigger men than you out of here for raising their voice. Sit.

Her captain drinks in the corner and laughs too loud at nothing. His crates for the garrison are in his ship's hold, at the mast. I send his supper up the mast-ladder of an evening, and last night, with the hatch open, I swear to you one of them said a name.
Evening. Mind the vats; the lime does not care who you are.
Tannery's shut. Nobody wants leather off a town that is turning to wood.
I have buried two apprentices this year. Try me.
The twins went down the culvert after their dog. Driftday last. I set a lamp in their window of a night. The key to the grate is on the nail inside; I have not had the stomach to turn it.
A tannery is the one trade that gets quieter the harder you work it. Should have been safe. Should have been.

ignatius.name: Ignatius Crane, Flambeau of the Pure Note

lines.text: The Note is held. You may speak under it. Quietly, and in tune.
This chapel had bells once. The Synod took them for bore-teeth, and it was right to. A bell is a voice with nobody inside it.
I have burned men for less than that tone. I am tired, and the Note is long, and you will not try me again.

Seven years I have held that it let go because one voice shouted. Vance's voice. The engineer says it let go because we held. I have thought about his answer every night since he gave it. I do not know yet which of us I would rather be right.

The warrant is read. The Pure Note is held over Oakhaven day and night until the casing. The Hollow behind the tannery is to be burned at the hour of the Rite. The Cantor is in the Church's protection, which is a phrase I chose myself, and I meant it, and it is a cell.
He has a glass arm that sings with the Note whether he wills it or not. I envied him that, for a moment, before I remembered what it is doing to him.
Mind the bed, twenty paces off the door. No sound carries over it for a day. Say what you came to say.
The hounds let you past. That means you came quietly. Good.
I don't build things anymore. I just know how they break. What do you want broken?

Revision Seven. My method, improved in an Arbiterium hand. Stage Nine is a four-hour hold at 174 with a collar and a wire. They did it at the Dawning Spire with forty singers for three hundred days. On the last morning the Light heard its own note held for it, and it asked a question, and it let go. I was there. I failed to stabilize it. That is the lie I tell.

It drinks what it breaks. Every Legionnaire I put down, the ring gets fuller and the tideline climbs. Three fingers from the shoulder, this morning. When it reaches the heart they call it Heartglass, and you become a humming statue, alive and aware.
If I carry all of it, no one else has to. I know what that sounds like. I'm an engineer; I know a bad load path when I draw one.
I laid my hand on it once. The humming stopped and something turned toward me. It is tired. It has been holding a lullaby for ten thousand years and it keeps losing the tune.
He is sitting with his back to the wreck, his glass arm across his knees, not looking at Lyra.
Seven forty-one is gone. I can hear the woods instead. They are very loud.
Not now.

Tuned stone. Every Cantor of the Memory Anchor, each in a tomb that rings the note they kept. Ring them in the order you would sing them home, high to low, and the choir opens. I know because I read the specification. I read all the specifications.
Listen. Under the water. Seven forty-one, very faint. The presses.
This is a dead city that never fell down. That is a statistical anomaly. I do not like anomalies.
My arm locks when that note is struck near it. Keep me away from the grey men, or keep them away from me.

The Memory Anchor. I calibrated its sister in the Dawning. Two percent survival at Stage Nine; I wrote the number down myself. I did not write down Whisper-Grove. I did not have to. It was in the next column.

Every press in the Office is tuned to a note I specified. I would like to see one. I would like to know how it works, so that I can learn how to stop one, and so that I stop dreaming about how it works.
...the lamps are late tonight...
...the lamps are late tonight...
...the lamps are late tonight...
She writes on her slate, in a hand as clear as print, and turns it round: "Read what you like. Quietly. The reeds are listening."
She writes: "The Conservatory. What is left of it. Sit, if you mean to read."
She writes one word, underlines it twice, and holds it up: "QUIETLY."
She writes, and it takes a while: "We taught the reed and the breath. Forty Cantors went out of this room. I kept the books because I could not keep the voices."

She writes: "The Debt of Overtone. Eleven years ago I sang one note too many for a dying boy. He lived. The note kept my voice. I would sing it again." She rubs it out with her sleeve before you can read it twice.
She writes: "My best pupil and my worst listener. She sings the way I used to. Tell her nothing I said."
She writes: "Older than the Synod. We sang the orchards. Ask the books, not me; they are less tired."
Everything here came up the river inside something else. Read on the stools; buy at the counter. A sovereign or two a book.
Broadsheets, novels, sermons, filth, hymnals. I do not judge, I only carry. Mind the lamp.
If you are from the lock, you have seen nothing. If you are not, you have still seen nothing.
Four papers on the Row, all libellous, one occasionally correct. They print what the Synod will not, and I bring it upstream in tea-chests. Nobody in the Reach drinks that much tea.
He reads everything I carry before I carry it, and sells what he reads. So I carry nothing he would want to sell. Mostly.
My best customer and my worst debtor. If you see him at the Boar, remind him what he owes me. Do not use the word "owes". He faints.
...on the left, by size... not by name... not by name...
...by size... the tall ones at the back... mind the spines...
...not by name...
He lifts a book from the bench and shelves it, carefully, by size. Then he takes it down again and shelves it again. "...somebody will want it..."
You came. Sit, keep your voice in your chest. I've a thing to ask that I should not ask anyone.
Come in, close the door. The lamp's lit; we can talk.
Lower. Please. There are things in this town that learn from every sound.

He was my shadow when we were children. He left at seventeen for the Conservatory of Bores and came back with an arm of glass and no words. He lives outside the Hedge because the hounds will not touch him, and because he has decided he does not deserve the inside.

Stage Nine: a four-hour unison hold at the casing. Source: Cantor, local. That is me. They will put a collar on my throat and a wire through my voice and I will sing the Root to sleep for them, and then they will drink it. Unless we break the bore first.
A martyr is just a musician who gave up before the coda. I would rather not be either.
She is sitting on a crate with her slate on her knees, listening to the trees.
She is listening north, toward the Mausoleum, with her whole body.
She does not look up.
She writes: MY FATHER'S OFFICE IS IN THE BOOK THERE. THEY BURIED THE TUNE WITH THE CANTORS.
She has no voice at all. She writes on a slate, and turns it to you.
She has no voice at all. She writes on a slate, and turns it to you.
She looks at you for a long moment, and does not write anything.
She writes: SEVENTY-FOUR THOUSAND. She underlines it. Then she rubs it out with her sleeve, because it is not a thing you can leave written down.
She writes: HE KEEPS A LIST ON A DECK-BEAM NOW. Then, smaller: SO DID THEY.
She watches your mouth, not your eyes, and nods once.
She watches your mouth. "Slower," she says. "I read lips, not minds."
She looks at you for a long moment and goes back to splicing one-handed.
"It hunts by sound. That horn on the bow hears a man breathe at a hundred yards. I don't make any." She grins. "Go quiet, or go fast, and kill the horn first. When it hears you, everybody hears you."
"My collarbone and her number-three tank. One of us will be flying in a week."

moor_bookseller.name: Bastien Corvo, pedlar of Cantabile broadsheets

lines.text: Dry pages, if you would like something to read. A Cantabile serial in two parts, a tale out of the Caldera. A sovereign a part, or read the Cantor’s lending copies for nothing.
Two parts, stitched, up the river from Broadsheet Row. Hetty keeps a paid-for bundle by the east table if coin is short.
Paper tears more easily than people think. So do manners. A sovereign a part, and keep it inside your coat.
The Cantor keeps lending copies on a shelf at her house. You can read both parts there without buying them. The bundle here was paid for by a carter: one of each for whoever wants to take them home.

Four papers on the Row, all libellous, one occasionally correct. This is none of the four. It is a tale, the names are changed, and that is the only reason it came up the river past Stillwater. The lockkeeper there reads everything I carry, and sells what he reads.
"...lilies for the Cantor... lilies..."
"...we're late... the bell hasn't gone..."
She walks past you with her lilies.
Hm-mm. All's well. Sit if you like; the stool next door is free.
Hm. Keep to the Narrow, love, and the street keeps you.
Lower. I am humming for the whole street, not for you.
Evening. Mind the pole. Every lamp in Oakhaven by full dark, and not one of them quiet.
Can't stop. Twenty-four lamps and one taper, and the dark does not wait on me.
Out of the way of the pole, if you would. Lamps first. Talk after.
He is not to be looked at. Whoever you are. He has a cough.
The mill is shut. Say what you want through the door next time.
Get out of my mill.

The Grafters posted the inspection on the Greenhall door. Every child under twelve, hands and feet, Rootday week. Rooke chalks the mark. After the mark they come for you with the saw, and they are kind about it.

Lyra hummed him through the night it started. Spent her whole voice on his hands. She had nothing left for Orla Hale in the morning, and Orla put out roots in her chair while Lyra sat there with her mouth open and nothing coming out.
Come closer, I cannot turn. Are you here about Davin?
Mind the roots on the floor. They are mine.
I am a tree with a tongue; shout at me if you like, I cannot leave.
I heard my son sing my harvest song at the Boar. And then I heard it sung back by something with nobody inside it. All the lines. Even the fourth.
Evening. If it is about a burial, I keep the book. If it is about anything else, I keep my voice down.
Salt for the paths, a spade for the rest. What do you need?
He looks you up and down the way a sexton measures.
"—so I numbered them instead. Nineteen. Keep talking."
"—and the grey one went broody in the spring— What."
"That's it. Loud is fine. Loud is alive."
I kept eleven. You name a hen and it dies, so I numbered them. Then I came here, and they numbered me.

Brass, nine feet across the mouth, under a lead hood. They don't throw shot. They throw noise. Forty of them, at dawn, out over the edge of the world, every day since the crack. We call it the Refusal.
Thirty yards of bare rock, and then the land stops. Don't look at it long. You can't, anyway. You'll find you're looking at your boots.

The only men on the Watch allowed to be silent. Lead over the face, hammered to fit, no holes in it. They stand along the lip and listen for us. When one of theirs starts to walk, the two beside him fetch him back. They don't fetch us.
"—and it grounds the halberd soft, every time. Because of the powder. It still knows about the powder."
"—nine days. Ten tomorrow."
"Shh— no. Not that. Sorry. Keep talking. Just not about that."

The Arbiterium left it with us when the old guns went out of use, to mind the powder. Six years it has walked the same nine paces. Nine days ago it stopped in the middle of them and said something about bread.
Through the barrack and down. Felts on. No flame, no shot, no iron on stone. It will not open the big door to anybody, but it has never thought to bar ours.
"—he could open a gate, that dog. Not push it. Open it. Evening. You're quiet. You want to watch that, here."
"—and the food, which is always worse. You're quiet. You want to watch that, here."
"Shout if you like. It all counts. It's the quiet ones we ring the bell for."

You go quiet on the Watch and somebody sounds the bell. Standing order. Nine. They don't look first. They don't ask. They just ring it. It's not a punishment. It's because the ones that go quiet are the ones that go.
Over. To listen. Near enough a hundred and eighty since the year of the crack, and every one of them went quiet first. So we talk.
Nothing that matters. Nobody on the Watch does. That's what talk is for. That's the whole trick of it. Onions. Days of the week. Counting cable-eyes. My dog.
Rufus. I had him as a boy in the Peaks. He'd lift the latch with his nose and walk the gate back, and then he'd sit down in the gap and look at you, as if you'd asked him to.
Up to the walk between Five and Six. Keep to the manned batteries till you've got the way of it. Eight's hooded this week. From Seven to Nine there's nobody but you.
"—my nan sang it. Every night. I'd know it in my sleep. I do know it in my sleep."
"—four lines. It only ever does three."
"Not so loud. Not about that."
A cradle-song. It is from where I am from, and I am not saying where. I wrote it out so I would stop hearing the gap at the end. It is in my locker, under the Sermon.
Because it stops at the third line, and waits, and then it starts again, and while it is doing that it is still here. Nobody knows what it does when it gets to the end.
"—two short, a pause, one long: that is yes. Sorry. Eighty-Eight. I was listening to her knuckles."
"—four flat: the Watch holds the wall. Everybody knows that one."
"If you are going to shout, shout something with a rhythm. I can use that."
Everybody learns the battery calls. I am learning the rest. There is nothing to do on the wall but talk and listen, so I talk with my mouth and listen with everything else.
In the Peaks. You would not know it. I would not know it now.
"—and that is a traveller, General, off the Coast skyship, and civil with it— Ninety-Four. I say what the General says."
"—and the bag is patched on the starboard side, General, a good deal— Yes? Ninety-Four."
"—and that one has a mouth on them, General. I would not, if I were you. She can hear tone."

It was the Fortis sappers' code, tapped on pipes in the deep galleries where a voice does not carry. She strikes it on the iron over her heart. Everybody on the Watch learns the battery calls. Almost nobody learns the whole of it. I have enough to say it after her.

That is my subject. Three sovereigns the cask at the Fenwick chandler's when I left, and four here, and the sutler says five by Frostmonth, and the wicks are extra. Nobody else may have lamp-oil. Ask on the roster.
In the Reach. I owed money there. You get the wall for a debt of that size. Three years, so far.
It is not an appointment. It is come by. The one before me talked about rope. When I stop, somebody will come up a stair and offer.
Nothing through there. Blankets. Keep talking and keep moving.
Move along. Keep talking.
Say that louder and I will have you counting cable-eyes till Frostmonth.
Shut for the damp. Nine days. It is routine, and it is on the sheet as routine.
Issue. Coat, mitts, spike. You sign with a mark if you can't sign.
Issue. What.
Issue. Mind your tone, or you can go on the wall in what you stand up in.
Lead plates, sewn in. It will not stop the quiet. Nothing stops the quiet but your own mouth. But it is the Watch's coat, and the Watch knows its own.
Not from me. The magazines keep their own, on a rack. You do not walk on powder in nails.
"—and that's her lines made fast, and that's the windlass pawled— Mind the ladder."
"—Coast-built, by the cut of her, and knocked about—"
"—and that one shouts. Good. Shout on the wall and you'll live."
Not many ships come. The Synod's packets, with the condemned, four times a year. A sutler's barge when the wind allows. You.
Keep talking. Stores are the other side of the Watch. This is Nine. Nothing here is for issue.
Keep talking.
Keep talking. Somewhere else.
In the Peaks. I hit an officer who had hit a boy. Spring of '13. They sent me to the end of the world for it. It had only just become the end.
Barred. It goes out onto the rock, to the buttress and the crane. Nobody goes out there without my leave, and you have not got it.
I can't. I can write my name and two words more. It has been enough.
Subject?
Number and subject. No number? Visitor, then. Subject.
Subject. I have four hundred of these to chalk before the hour.
Read the board. Pick one of the visitors' four. Keep to it. If you dry up on the wall, say the days: nobody has ever run out of days.
A lantern and a tin. Whoever sat there last leaves a note for whoever sits there next, and you read it out. It does not matter what it says. It matters that it gets said.
Somebody sits by every bunk and talks, to keep the sleeper's breathing company. Two hours on. It is the kindest duty on the roster and the dullest.
"—and then you take your onions, and you want them sliced thin, not chopped, thin, and you want a heavy pan—"
"—thin, I said, and a heavy pan—"
"—that's the way, good and loud, now the pan—"
Standing Order Nine. You get used to it. The new ones can't sleep for a month, and after that they can't sleep anywhere else.
"—forty-one, forty-two, forty-three, and that's the cable-eyes on the north face of Six done, now the south face, forty-four—"
"—forty-four, forty-five— don't make me lose my place— forty-six—"
"—forty-seven! Forty-eight! See, I can do it loud as well—"
The iron eyes the cable runs through. Somebody counts them every watch. If the count comes out different, either an eye has gone or the counter has, and both are worth knowing.
"—told her, I said, you can have the blue or you can have the green, but you can't have both and expect your mother not to say something—"
"—the blue, in the end. Obviously the blue—"
"—and she had a voice on her like yours, as it happens—"
She shouted her voice to rags that first night. Shouted it to bits, and the bits went over the edge, and she's never had it back. Now, the thing with gravy—
"—Rootday, Hearthday, Massday, Stasisday, Dawnday, Driftday, Memoryday, Nullday, Rootday, Hearthday—"
"—Massday, Stasisday, Dawnday—"
"—Driftday! Memoryday! Nullday! Go on, you take the next round—"
It's the easiest subject there is. You can't run out. You get to Nullday and there's Rootday again, waiting for you.
(She strikes her breastplate with her knuckles: twice, sharp; a long flat blow; three quick taps.) "The General says, welcome to Null-Watch. The General says, keep talking."
(Two short blows, a pause, one long.) "The General says, state your ship and your business, and say it aloud, and go on saying something after."
(She does not strike the iron at all. Ninety-Four fills the gap.) "The General is waiting for you to say that again, in another way."
(Four flat heavy blows.) "The General says, the Watch holds the wall. The General says, the Watch holds the wall and nothing else."
"The General says the Watch obeys the Synod when the Synod is not mad. The General says the Synod has been mad since the spring of 413."

"The General says nothing about that." (Ninety-Four goes on, in the same voice.) "Spring of 413. The batteries were new and nobody knew how to lay them. She laid them by voice, tower to tower in the dark, for thirty-one hours. At dawn on the second day she opened her mouth to say cease firing, and nothing came out."

(One blow, struck hard enough to ring.) "The General says, keep talking. On the wall, in the yards, on the stairs. The General says, if you go quiet somebody will ring a bell, and they will not look first."
"—and then your sister wrote, and the calf was a heifer after all— I can do both. Go on."
"—in, and out, that's it, and the calf—"
"Wake him and you take the next two hours."
You talk to their breathing. In, and out. If it changes, you talk closer. It has never failed yet in this hall, and nobody wants to be the one it fails for.
Garrow Finch, on a crate in the cellar, nudges a stool out with his boot. "Hetty's board says no dice, and Hetty's board is upstairs. A throw of bones, if you have a coin to lose?"
Garrow Finch, a quarry hauler off shift, shakes his cup inside his coat so it will not rattle. "Bones? One to twenty sovereigns. Nobody down here ever got rich, and nobody has had to leave."
"Bones, or back up the stair," says Garrow, and shakes the cup inside his coat.
Flume eel, the green sort. Do not worry about the colour. It is only the water.
Eel or nothing.
You smell of the Hedge. Buy an eel and I will forget.
Willow-bark, reed-pith, moss. Cut this morning, so it still remembers being green.
Herbs. Bandage-stuff, if you bleed.
Handle it or buy it. It bruises.
Eat something. You have the look of someone who has been listening too hard.
Honey, eel, tonic. Eat first, ask after.
Buy or stop breathing on the pies.
A little of everything, and the everything is mostly quiet.
Reeds, bottles, pebbles. Do not ask what the pebbles are for.
Look, do not breathe on it.
Mending, selling, sharpening. Mostly selling.
Edges and shot. Do not ask where the shot came from.
If it is loud, I do not stock it.
Softly, love. New flour, the first in a year that tastes of nearly what it should. Bread, cider, curd. Eat it while it is warm.
Hearth bread, cider, moot-curd. Last Sheaf week. Market prices; I am not here to get rich.
If you are going to shout, buy something first, and shout into the bread.
We bake for the Last Sheaf every year the field is cut. This year the dough is rising and nobody has told the Church.
Flour does not mind the Hedge. Flour minds the damp.
Not here. Not now. Ask Harrow.
Not now. Ask Harrow.
Hush. Ask Harrow, and ask him quietly.
Blessings of the Pure Note, citizen. Take a place in the square. There is bread after. There is always bread after.
The Rite is a festival. Festivals are attended.
Lower your voice. This is a feast, and feasts are quiet.
A feast for the whole district. Attendance is a courtesy and will be noted.

p13h_wenna.name: Bethan Marl, neighbour to the Tarrows

lines.text: Softly, if you would. I stand out here because I cannot sit in there.
Does it ring? Not next door, it does not. Keep your voice down.
If you mean to shout, shout at your own door.

Gil cut reeds. Maud kept the carders' books. Linnet is eight and counts everything she walks past. Nan was Gil's mother, and the oldest voice in this lane. They went out on the last cart before the gate was barred.
Tuned to you before you can lift your head, and hung over the door. Every reed in this lane stirs a little when the wind comes through the Hedge. The Tarrows' hang still. The wind goes round them.
It keeps every sound this town ever made. It has your first cry and your mother's last word, and it gives them back when it likes, in whatever voice it was given. That is the only mercy in it.

When one of us is dying the family holds their pitch until the body lets go, and counts it out in eights, one for each Anchor. On the eighth, the note is let go. We do it in silence now. It is not that we are afraid. It is that it does not carry.
Nessa Tolliver, a ferrywoman off the Flume, shuffles a worn deck with one hand. "Evening. A round of Rounds, if you have the patience?"
Nessa Tolliver shuffles twenty-four cards with the ease of someone who has done it on a moving boat. "Rounds. Two to thirty sovereigns. I only cheat the river."
"Rounds, or the next seat," says Nessa, and cuts the deck.
Good day. The Consortium draws letters of credit here, payable to the bearer. Five in the hundred on cashing. Quietly, please; the Factor is at the next desk.
Letters of credit. Gold in, paper out. Do not unfold one near the lamp.
If you want to shout, shout at the Factor. If you want a letter, speak low.
You are welcome at the desk. It is not much of a desk. Everything on it is kept.
Ledger-keeper. If it is paper, I will read it. If it is owed, I will write it down.
Raised voices are written down too. Shall I begin?
Peace, under the Note. Sit, if there is a place. We begin when the last of us has stopped talking.
The Note is held. There is a place at the end of the bench, if you want it.
Lower your voice. This is a listening, and you are in the middle of it.
We are not here to frighten anyone. A frightened town sings out of tune, and a held town sings one note, and the quiet has nothing to take.
Hearthday. Attendance is a courtesy. I would come. It will be a long note.
You came along the Flume road on foot? Under the Wash? Then you timed it. Good. The last man who did not is still being walked back down.
Mind the planks. They are not all as old as they look.
Not now.
Do not tell me where it came from. I will tell you what it is worth, and it is less than you hoped.
Half. Half of what a clean shop pays, and no questions.
Put it on the board or put it back.
Does it ring? No. Nothing rings on this wharf, that is the trouble.
Forty logs and a chained lock.
If you are not here about the wheel, you are in the way of the wheel.
Lock dues in advance, friend. Or a coin for the news. Or both. Everyone does both.
You have the look of someone who wants to know something. It is twelve sovereigns, or the tide, whichever turns first.
Quietly. The basin carries.
My man poles the raft. The wheel has been shut since spring. The Compact blames the lock, the lock blames the keeper, the keeper blames the weather. It is a very cold way to run a river.
We are out of tea, patience and luck, in that order.
Mind your feet near the edge.
Does it ring? True enough, if you keep it low. I write letters for people who cannot, and I sit where the Chapel can see me, so nobody says I hide it.
Does it ring? I write letters. Forty-one since the gate was barred. Not one has had an answer.
If you want a letter written, say what to put in it. If you want to shout, the Hedge will oblige.
Oh. You are not on the sheet. Please do not tell Corporal Pike I looked up. I am owed four months and I have forgotten how it feels to sit down.
Counting-room. Staff only. I did not see you. I am writing.
I have not got a penny and I have not got a minute. Go away.
The Reeve-Moot is always glad of an honest petitioner. Sit, sit.
Alder Mossbrook. Reeve. You will forgive me if I do not stand; the moot ran long.
I have a good deal to do, and none of it is you.
The Chapel is open to all who keep to the Note. Mind the step.

There's talk, on the upper tiers, where the Tiers go up to the line to scavenge. They say there's something up in the Bleach that isn't Wired. Something that moves at night on the chains. With wings. The Tiers call it the black angel. They leave food out for it on the line.
I keep the Free Captains' business in the Keel Docks. A letter from Oona Salt gets you through my door. Without one, you are buying rope.

p92_canvas.name: The woman under the black canvas

lines.text: Under the canvas, quick. What do you need that you cannot buy in the light?
Looking, or buying?
Loud. Go and be loud somewhere else.

The only one in the Tiers, and it stays under the cloth. Mirrors are illegal. A reflection is a second light, and the Light is jealous. You want it, you buy it covered, and you never take the cloth off down here.
Every window painted black on the inside, and every family scratches one sign in the paint. A bird, a name, a sun. At dusk the scratch-light tells you whose house it is.
Light keep you true.
Shh.
Quiet. Please.
We do not go above the line. Some go up for what the noble houses left, with a black cloth on a pole. Not all come down.

p92_joss.name: Joss Feveril, of the seventh chain

lines.text: Light keep you true. Seventh chain. Mind the walk.
Crew. Seventh chain.
Talk like that on a chain-walk and the chain will answer you.
Children learn the nine links by name before they learn their letters. The chain you are on decides which way you run when one jerks.
Every crewman wears one. A notch for every man you lost. One in nine of us, Bardo says. He keeps a tally of nineteen in his winch housing.
The seventh chain's cage runs from the anchor-house down past the bell-gallery to the docks. Somebody pinned it up top, years back. Knock the pin out from up there and it comes down.
Name. Cargo. Quietly: we speak in the Narrow here.
You came up on that airship. Keep your voice down and your feet in the shade.
Speak like that again and the whole dock will look at you. Nobody here looks at anybody.
The freighters come into the cradles, and the ladders go up from here. Everything the city eats comes past me, and I count it.
Up the face, where the black wall is. Above it, the Bleach. Below it, us. Seven years we have lived on the undersides, and we are good at it.
The one ahead owns their shadow and lends it. Step out of somebody's shade without a word and you have insulted them. Give your shade to a stranger and you have done the finest thing you can do here.
The shade-lamp at my door. Sit by it when you come back down, and you will be whole again. Everybody comes back down.
Your mirrors. Your sextant. Your shaving-glasses, your hand-mirrors, any lens that shows a face. A reflection is a second light. The Light is jealous. They'll be returned when you leave the chains.
Light keep you true, and keep your boots off my brake.
Whose are you? Never mind. Touch nothing that has a handle.
Low-pitched, loud-footed, lamp-blind son of a slack link. Speak in the Narrow, or go up and shout at the Bleach.
Nineteen men, to jerking tethers. I cut each one in the housing, where I have to look at it. I do not say their names in here. The chains know them.

The nine come down out of the sky to the rim, through the rings, and on down through the frame to the keel. The city's bones. Since the light took the rim we cannot get at them from on top, so we keep them from underneath.

The city sways, and the bones take it one after another, never two together. Count the row. When the seventh speaks, be standing on a pin. A link under a speaking chain will throw a man, and it does not care which.
The seventh's goods-cage. I pinned it up top myself, after the nineteenth, and may whoever knocks that pin out come back as a link on the wet side.

Below the weights, in the keel, where the nine are made fast. The old capstan. Nobody has worked it since before my time, and it turns. I have nineteen strokes up here, and I have stood at the top of that stair and heard nineteen men hauling. I do not go down.
Light keep you true. Mind the hems, they are clean.
Seven years I have had nobody to robe. Stand still and let me see the length of you.
You cast, I will say that for you. Do not drip on the linen.

Four hundred. I wash every one each spring and hang it back on its peg, and nobody has put one on since the Fracture but the choir. In the old days the whole city went out at dawn in these. You walked out over the gulf with the Spire on your right hand, shining, and you sang.

A kilometre, almost level, and not a roof on it but the cage. The Tiers teach it to their children as soon as they can walk: walk in the shade of the one ahead of you. If there is no one ahead of you, run.

Black silk on black poles. The Altar's people go out under them every day, the choir before dawn and the clerics after it to polish the Eye, like a procession of black mushrooms. Keep under one and the light goes on round you. Step out, and it begins.

Two upstairs, keeping the winch. They let choir and bearers out of the mouth and nobody else. They look at the robe. They have never once looked at a face. Past the cage it is the Brother-Captain's half, Aurel Sant's. His men walk it in their own fire: the white parts round glass-fire.

The white never goes out. But when the sun is up there are two lights on the chain, and the two together are more than anything can stand in. Go by night. Go at the dead hour if you can: it lies thinnest then.

Bronze, forty feet across, at the back of the Altar. The only mirror in the Heights that is not a crime. It has gone white like everything, all but the middle, where they polish it every day with oil and ash. I have not seen it in seven years. I can tell you exactly what it looks like.
Light keep you true.
State your office.
Low-pitched. Speak up, or go back down the hole you came out of.
Choir and bearers. Nobody else has walked the chain since the Fracture, and nobody else will while this winch is kept.
Brother-Captain Sant has the far end, and the steps. His fire has not dipped in seven years. Ask him what yours is doing.
There is one note. The second note is sin.
Light keep you true.
Light keep you true. Sit, if you like, and keep the note company.
Light keep you true. In this room we speak softly, and we listen.
Every soul holds one true note. Sin is the note going flat. Grace is the note held.
The Church teaches that the second note is sin.
We taught under the east window, before. We teach here now.
Light keep you true.
Light keep you true. Speak low, please. I am practising.
You are very loud. Out there they would call that low-pitched.
I am holding it. The Cantor says if I hold it every night it will hold itself.
We may sing here. Out there nobody speaks above the Narrow.
Light keep you true. You came up a long way to see snow.
Light keep you true. You came up a long way to see snow.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
She was here before any of us. She does not sleep much, and she will not be thanked.
Twelve of us. There were more once. Nobody comes up the mountain to join now.
Light keep you true. Speak softly. The Abbess is resting.
Light keep you true. Speak softly. The Abbess is resting.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
Twelve of us. There were more once. Nobody comes up the mountain to join now.
It does not go off the peaks, not even at the end of summer. We melt it for water.
Light keep you true. Sit, if you like. There is only the cot.
Light keep you true. Come in, and shut the door. The cold gets into everything.
Light keep you true, all the same.
Coriel. I am the Abbess of this house. There are twelve of us left. I am the oldest.
I watched it. From the tower you can see the Spire, on a clear morning. Three hundred sunrises I stood up there and watched, and I did nothing. That is all there is to say about it.
We ring it at dusk. It is the only thing that works.
Something comes up the cliffs every night, out of the dark below. The bell holds it while it rings. If you go down by the postern, be up before the last stroke.
Light keep you true. Are you hurt? Then go to the Abbess, not to me.
Light keep you true. Are you hurt? Then go to the Abbess, not to me.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
I keep the infirmary. Chilblains, mostly, and the old cough. Up here the cold is the only enemy you can see.
She gives away what she needs. I scold her for it, and she does it again the next day.
Light keep you true. Mind the ice on the step.
Light keep you true. Mind the ice on the step.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
Ring the bell on the post and somebody comes. Most of the winter nobody rings it at all.
We do not get many. A ship on the shelf is a thing we talk about for a month.
Light keep you true. Watch the sky. It changes fast up here.
Light keep you true. Watch the sky. It changes fast up here.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
She was here before any of us. She does not sleep much, and she will not be thanked.
Light keep you true. Walk on the flags. The garth is deep.
Light keep you true. Walk on the flags. The garth is deep.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
On a clear morning you can see it from the tower, a white needle a long way off. You can see the crack in it. We do not look at it much.
Light keep you true. Do not lean on the parapet.
Light keep you true. Do not lean on the parapet.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
She was here before any of us. She does not sleep much, and she will not be thanked.
Light keep you true. We are not used to new faces.
Light keep you true. We are not used to new faces.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
Sister Ottavia rings it at dusk. Whatever comes up the cliffs stops while it rings.
On a clear morning you can see it from the tower, a white needle a long way off. You can see the crack in it. We do not look at it much.
Light keep you true. Do not touch the rope.
Light keep you true. Do not touch the rope.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
Twelve strokes at dusk. While it rings, whatever comes up the cliffs lets go of the rock. When it stops, it does not.
It is mine to ring. My hands know the weight of it, and the bell knows my hands.
Light keep you true. Shut the gate behind you, when you go.
Light keep you true. Shut the gate behind you, when you go.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
She was here before any of us. She does not sleep much, and she will not be thanked.
Light keep you true. The wind is from the south today.
Light keep you true. The wind is from the south today.
You are loud for a mountain. Light keep you true, all the same.
On a clear morning you can see it from the tower, a white needle a long way off. You can see the crack in it. We do not look at it much.
She was here before any of us. She does not sleep much, and she will not be thanked.
Light keep you true. You are a long way up for a stranger.
Light keep you true. Mind the line. It does not look like anything.
Speak low or go down.
There, where the dark stops. Things left on it are not ours and not yours. Past it you go from shadow to shadow and you do not dawdle between.
He goes up every night, further than any of us, to the old market. He counts the ones who are still standing in it. Ask him why. He will tell you somebody should.
Go at night. The dead hour if you can wait for it. Wrap your face and glove your hands. And keep quiet on the third tier: that street belongs to the choir.

There is a ring in the wall at the east end of the shelf. The line that goes on it is up in the garden, coiled on the parapet. Whoever gets up there by the streets can let it down, and after that it is one climb.
Light keep you true. Keep your voice where mine is.
Light keep you true. Low. They are two streets down.
Low. Or go and be loud somewhere I am not.

Every night. I stand here and I count them, and I cut it on the pole, and I chalk it on the pillar. Fourteen. Thirteen. A long while at thirteen. Nine tonight. Nobody comes for them. They are only less, a little at a time, the way a gull goes in that light.
It was a market on the morning it happened. You can see what they were doing. One was taking a coin. I do not know their names. I used to make names for them, and I stopped.

They do not hear words. They hear noise. Run, and they hear you. Strike something, and they hear you. Sing, and they will come up a house to find the mouth it came out of. Walk, and keep your voice in your chest, and you are a wall to them.
Shadow to shadow, the way you cross a river on stones. Every shadow up here lies north. The dead hour is the kindest. By day I would not put my hand out of that arcade.
The street is shut above the market. I have not looked for a way round. Things live on the chains. I leave them be, and they leave the count be.

p9_ada.name: Ada Pellow, widow of Cooper's Row

lines.text: Good day to you. Softly. I sit out here more, now, under it. It does not sound, but I like to be under it.
Does it ring? True enough, I suppose. Keep it low.
I have buried a husband and I have hung his reed twice. I will not be shouted at on my own step.
Seventy years in one parish. It was louder when I was a girl. Everything was.
Joram went in 418. The family holds the note until the body lets go, and in the old days it was sung out after. It cannot be now. The Hedge eats a note before it is halfway to the door.
Does it ring? True enough. The wagon is loaded, and it hums, and I find I am used to it.
The wagons do not creak any more. They hum. You feel it through the seat. A man could miss a creak.
I have one good hand and a bad temper. Choose which you want to speak to.
Timber comes out of the clearing and goes into the town, and the Hedge takes the noise off it at the gate. I have wondered where the noise goes.
The Synod counts timber by the load. It does not count what the load weighs on a man.
Shh. Mam says I'm not to talk to anybody about my hands.
I'm not supposed to be out. Don't tell.
Something whistled my whistle from the culvert. Only me and Lyra know my whistle. I didn't go. I nearly went.
Hot water? There is always hot water. Sit; the chair is clean. People hesitate less when the chair is clean.
You are not on my list, which means you are on someone else's. Sit down.
Lower your voice. There are people being registered in the next room, and it upsets them.

We do not harvest, whatever the pamphlets in the Reach say. We relieve. A man walks out of the Greening with his whole life on his back and nowhere to put it down. We take it from him. Most of them look relieved at six seconds.
Seventy-four thousand, and not one of them filed. The Hush did that, not us. We are the only people who ever came back to write them down.
Sable. I taught her to rule a page. Ruler, nib, blotter; she had the straightest hand I ever saw. She designed the harvest schedule herself, you know. I only signed it.
I have cut more limbs than any butcher in the Reach and done every one with care. Sit. I will not chalk your door today.
The sap-mark means past cutting. Now it also means the Inquisitor's list. Keep that to yourself.
Lower your voice in my surgery or I will lower it for you with a needle.
The Synod sends the saws. I hold them. Somebody has to hold them who will stop when the patient asks. The Inquisitor has asked for my list of sap-marks. I have been slow to find it.
Entry: the Deep Woods. One wreck, twenty-six souls, a press, and me.
Two things left in the inventory, and the third does not feel like a gap. It feels like a shelf.
I am counting. Wait.

A courier-cutter cannot carry anything heavier than paper and proctors. She was not carrying; she was listening, to four hundred and thirty-two cores murmuring in our hold. If there is anything under her hatch it is evidence: the Office seizes vox-bottles off the Rust Coast boats. If you open that hold, do not unstopper them in the dark. Quiets come through an open bottle like water through a sluice.
Entry: the stranger is polite in a drowned city. Noted.
I am a list, not a cure.
Precision, please. I record everything, including the tone.
I did not merely sign the catalogue. I designed the harvest schedule. I made it efficient. That is what I was good at.
Entry: the Hush does not take names. It takes the people and leaves the names lying about, like coats. The Catalogue only learned to pick them up.
I have read his calibration records. Two percent survival at Stage Nine. He wrote that number himself, in a very steady hand, and then he went and lived outside a hedge.
I hold the manifests for every core that captain has carried. Eleven consignments. I know the total. He does not want to. One day I will read it to him, one name at a time.
Stage Nine of the Vance Sequence. I filed it. The Cantor goes down in white because I wrote 'in white' on the form, so that she would not be mistaken for staff.
Entry: the subject asks the subject about the subject. Sable is a Veil designation. My own name is one of the three things I have left, and I do not spend it on strangers.
Crystallized song. A voice, bled out and set. I can read the name off a core the way you would read a label off a jar. That is what the Veil trained me for.

Two hundred and six Hollows in the Sunken Court. I read twenty names a night. Ten years and two hundred and twenty days to finish, and then you start again, because by then the first ones have stopped answering to them.
"...one more before the light goes... one more..."
"...deep enough... not deep enough... one more..."
He does not stop digging.
Sit if you like. She comes on the water about this time. You will hear her if you keep still.
Hm. You are standing where I listen.
Lower your voice. She will not come if you shout.

My Essa. Forty years dead, near enough; the pox took her the year the old king went into the glass. She used to call me Tammy. Nobody else ever did, before or since. And now something out past the thorn calls me Tammy, three or four nights in the eight, and three nights ago it came up the Flume in her voice, singing The Miller's Daughter, which is ours. Mine and hers.
Everyone says never answer it. I know what they say. I say she gets the second verse right, and the Hedge could not know the second verse.
Night shift. Keep it under the pumps and the bells won't turn. Are you — are you with him? With Engineer Vance?
Nobody comes down here who isn't on the roster. Which you aren't.
Quiet! The Legionnaire in Depot Three walks when it hears boots.
I learned the Vance Sequence at fourteen. I asked its author to sign my copy. He did. Then he looked at it for a long time and told me to keep the charts somewhere the Factor would not look.
Don't touch that. Or that. That one you can touch, it's already broken.
Number-three tank. Look at it. I could weep. I nearly have.
I'm an engine man in a forest. Say something useful or hold this.

Three bolts of silk to close the hole and a relief valve to stop her bursting the patch the first time Vane gets clever. Then hops. Forty miles, down, cool the tank, forty miles. It'll be like crossing a river on stepping-stones, if the stones were on fire.
Evening. Keep it low.
Hm?
Lower your voice before something hears you.
Blessings of the Narrow on you. Softly, now.
Yes? Quietly.
Hush! The children.

umber.name: Umber, a runaway of the Veil

lines.text: Entry: a stranger, polite, at the wrong end of the continent. Sit. Not there. That is where the proctors will come from.
I am a day-book, not a cure. Say what you came to say.
Precision, please. I was trained to record everything, including the tone.
I copied the harvest schedule fair, fourteen times, in a straight hand. Sable designed it. I only made it legible. That is what I was good at.
Entry: the Hush does not take names. It takes the people and leaves the names lying about, like coats. The Catalogue only learned to pick them up.
I have seen his calibration records; Sable kept them. Two percent survival at Stage Nine, in a very steady hand. He lives outside a hedge now, and I am told the hounds will not touch him.
Eleven consignments to Whisper-Grove. The archivist there holds the manifests and knows the total. I copied the totals and did not add them up. One day she will read it to him, one name at a time.
Stage Nine of the Vance Sequence. Sable filed it. I ruled the lines on the form. 'In white' is in her hand, so that the Cantor would not be mistaken for staff.

Umber is a Veil designation, as Sable is. She is the last archivist of the Silent Veil, and she is in Whisper-Grove, reading names to the drowned, twenty a night. I was her junior. I could not stay and read with her, and I could not leave either, so I am here, which is neither.
Crystallized song. A voice, bled out and set. I can read the name off a core the way you would read a label off a jar. That is what the Veil trained me for.
Every sailor dies, friend. The trick is to be somewhere else when it happens. Sit; I'm buying, because I'm frightened.
Corsair, Rust Coast, retired from the sea on account of the sea. What'll you have?
Ha! You have the look of somebody about to tell me something I already know and have been drinking not to hear.
Bought with money I'd rather not discuss, from people I'd rather not name. She holds eighteen if nobody's fat and she lifts with three tanks.
I carry one. Labelled with a name I won't say. Almost certainly a fake. I have never unstopped it, and I think about it every night.
Twelve crates of replacement cores for the quarry garrison. I don't ask what's in them. I have been very carefully not asking for two years. It is a skill.
Ten heartbeats. I counted. This time I didn't cut.
She's on her side in the willows with a hole in her number-three tank you could post a sheep through. We are not leaving by air today.
Don't. I know. I put a tree through an Office cutter. It seemed like the thing to do.

She'll fly. Forty-mile hops, if Tobiah can close the tank and stop the seam weeping. Further than that, she needs a whole new lift-tank, and there's only one coast that sells them without asking whose ship it is.

She went down east of here with the willow-crown in her bow. Her listening-horn will still be working; those things outlive their crews. It was our hold she was listening to. Four hundred and thirty-two, murmuring. We're a bell. I've been ringing it for two years.
North. Big marble thing in a ring of graves. The Cantor wants to go there. I'm not going to be the man who tells the Cantor no.
Mind the ladder; the third rung is a liar. She'll hold at the mast-height as long as the tanks do, and the tanks are not what they were.
OK-114, under two coats of paint. She's initialled it eleven times, your scribe. I can tell by the way she looks at my hull.
Say it quick. I don't like a city that doesn't fall down.
Twenty-one souls, a hold that murmurs, and a lift-tank with a weep in the seam. She'll get us off this water. Further than that I won't promise anybody.

One thousand three hundred and forty-two. I know the number now. I didn't want to; somebody made me hear it. The Office has me in a file under "reliable, does not ask questions." I am asking questions now. Loudly.
I've flown over it twice with cargo. Never put down. You don't, here. The Hollows walk out across the water toward the ladder like they've been waiting for a ship, and then they walk back.

vosk.name: Factor Adela Vosk, Consortium of Bores

lines.text: Pitch has a colour, through these lenses. Yours is an unremarkable brown. State your business.
The Consortium pays this town's bread. Remember that before you speak.
I have Legionnaires. You have a voice. One of those is replaceable.
Stage Nine. Source: Cantor, local, one. Collar: standard. Wire: standard. It is a procedure, not a sacrifice. The Church likes the robes; we like the yield.
A resource. It will yield without limit if correctly relieved. That is the Arbiterium's phrasing, not mine, and I confess I do not entirely follow it.
She does not stop singing.
She does not stop singing.
She does not stop singing.
"Hello," she says, very loudly, and then, remembering, much more quietly: "hello."
"Hello," she says, very loudly, and then, remembering, much more quietly: "hello."
She looks at you, and at your weapon, and decides you are all right.
"They don't talk. Mam said that's holy. Mam said if I sang nice the Quiet would come and be kind to me." She thinks about it. "It wasn't going to be kind, was it."
"She's teaching me the skipping one. Too loud brings the hounds, too still brings the Hush." She hops, twice, very softly. "You have to be in the middle. That's called the Narrow."
